articles.title: What survivors America’s deadliest mass shooting remember hints at something surprising about memory under threat
articles.summary: Many survivors of the Route 91 Harvest Festival shooting described people helping under fire in as much detail as the gunfire itself, a finding that surprised researchers who expected the accounts to center almost entirely on threat.

articles.title: Dark personalities and flawed logic drive antisocial behavior on separate tracks
articles.summary: A new study finds that while dark personality traits and cognitive biases both predict rule-breaking behavior, they do not feed into one another. The findings suggest different psychological pathways can lead to delinquency.

articles.title: Many new mothers struggle with birth-related trauma symptoms even without meeting criteria for PTSD
articles.summary: How common is birth trauma? A standardized survey of new mothers in 31 countries found an average of 23% described their birth as traumatic, though rates in individual countries ranged from 7% to 69%.

articles.title: Over 10 percent of factual claims in Google’s AI search summaries aren’t backed by their cited sources, study finds
articles.summary: Google’s AI Overviews provide direct answers to billions of searchers, but a new analysis reveals that one in nine generated claims lacks source support. The system also bypasses traditional search rankings, threatening the revenue of original web publishers.

articles.title: Extra weight may be aging your brain faster than you think
articles.summary: A major 24-year study involving more than 8,200 adults suggests that excess body weight may accelerate brain aging, leading to faster declines in memory, concentration, and decision-making skills. The connection was particularly strong among people over 65, raising concerns about the long-term effects of obesity on brain health.

articles.title: Scientists find surprisingly little evidence that medical cannabis helps you sleep
articles.summary: A major new review challenges the growing enthusiasm for medical cannabis as an insomnia treatment, finding little reliable evidence that it improves sleep quality, sleep duration, or daytime functioning. Researchers caution that this doesn't mean cannabis is ineffective, only that existing studies are too weak to establish whether it works.

articles.title: Common pesticide linked to 2.5 times the risk of Parkinson’s disease
articles.summary: A UCLA study found that long-term exposure to a common pesticide was linked to more than 2.5 times the risk of Parkinson's disease. Scientists also uncovered how the chemical damages brain cells and identified a promising way to protect them.

articles.title: Scientists use sound waves to deliver a new attack on deadly brain cancer
articles.summary: Scientists at the University of Virginia have developed a promising new strategy to fight glioblastoma, one of the deadliest and most difficult-to-treat forms of brain cancer. Their experimental approach combines focused ultrasound, tiny nanoparticles, and genetic molecules called microRNAs to attack multiple cancer-driving genes simultaneously.

articles.summary: arXiv:2610.40700v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: To rigorously establish the value of a novel deep learning method, it must be compared against appropriate baselines. In this work, we investigate whether this problem can be mitigated by using large language models to automate the construction of baselines. articles.title: Bayesian Distribution System State Estimation with Flow Matching
articles.summary: arXiv:2610.40728v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Medium-voltage feeders have few real-time measurements, so distribution system state estimation (DSSE) rests on pseudo-measurements of the secondary substations, a prior in Bayesian terms. Weighted least squares keeps the power flow exact but reduces this prior to a mean and variance, while supervised deep learning estimators also learn the power flow and are tied to one measurement set. We propose PoSE (posterior sampling for state estimation), which keeps the Bayesian structure of DSSE and learns only what the distribution system operator does

articles.title: Don't Just Impute, Detect: Task-Aware Diffusion Pipelines for Edge Anomaly Detection
articles.summary: arXiv:2610.40732v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT) edge pipelines routinely lose contiguous blocks of multi-sensor data to network dropouts and hardware faults. The standard remedy is a disjointed "impute-then-detect" pipeline whose imputer is trained only for Mean Squared Error (MSE). Such an imputer fills a missing block with the most probable normal pattern: a partially observed anomaly is smoothed back toward normality, and boundary artifacts on normal data raise false alarms. We call this imputation bias and propose the Task-Aware Diffusion Refiner (TADR)
